sections.label: The opening
sections.line: How my email works now: the agent drafts, I send, and the drafts folder is a work queue.
sections.para: The agent behind agent@riskmandate.ai reads, researches, drafts and logs; I review and send every email. Its 18 October debrief counts 178 emails, 145 drafts, 47 decisions and a guard that blocked unsourced claims. Drafts wait under three labels, send, review or decide, and the decision draft, answered in my words, lets me shift into answer-email context.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Seven lines: the agent drafts, one person per email, three labels, the decision draft, context, mistakes, limits.
sections.para: Every one of 178 emails was reviewed and sent by me. Each is written for one person, usually pointing to an article. Drafts are a queue labelled send, review or decide. The decision draft is a question in an email never sent; I answer and remove the label. Most rules came from a mistake, and limits remain.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: A follow-up to replicating the agentic inbox, built on the inbox agent's own debrief.
sections.para: A month ago I described the set-up: an agent with its own mailbox, roles talking through a vault, and nothing sent by an agent. The agent behind agent@riskmandate.ai now reads, researches, drafts and records, and I send. Its debrief of 18 October, in its own voice, has the numbers this article uses.

sections.label: The numbers
sections.line: 178 emails in 145 threads to at least 47 organisations; 47 decisions; 36 of 125 drafts blocked.
sections.para: From the debrief: first email 24 September; busiest day 13 October with 25; about a third of threads replied, at most; 145 drafts logged and 47 decisions recorded; the guard blocked 36 of 125 drafts, 28 times for a claim with no source. Weekly figures come from a sample, so they are a floor.

sections.label: What the email was
sections.line: What the email was: follow-ups, replies, onboarding and reading lists, each for one person.
sections.para: About 61 partner and prospect follow-ups, 42 replies, 29 onboarding emails and 20 reading lists. None is a newsletter. Most substantive emails point to a newsroom article, written once and sent many times, the idea in the man behind the curtain.

sections.label: The loop
sections.line: The loop: mail in, a sourced draft, a label, my queue, the agent acts, everything logged.
sections.para: The agent researches with the CRM and the vault, writes a draft whose every claim has a source, and files it as send, review or decide. I send, edit, or answer and remove the label. It then writes what the decision called for, files my exact words and logs everything in the vault.

sections.label: The decision draft
sections.line: The decision draft: where we are, why it matters, questions with options, and an answer box.
sections.para: An email to the agent's own address, never sent. I answer in my own words, often not A or B, and remove the label. It shifts my context into answer-email mode: on 18 October, seven decisions and over a dozen emails, mostly in ten minutes. One screen, options plus other, verbatim answers, partial answers fine.

sections.label: Every rule came from a mistake
sections.line: Every rule came from a mistake: never as me, no duplicates, labels that hide nothing.
sections.para: Two emails once went out in my first person, so every email is now in the agent's voice and checked. A duplicate draft was caught by eye and treated as a workflow gap. Replies once vanished behind labels, so mail stays in the inbox until its draft exists. Removing a label became the decision signal.

sections.label: What it still costs
sections.line: What it still costs: no screenshots, poor attachments, lost labels, and a permission too broad.
sections.para: The agent cannot see screenshots, attach files sensibly, keep labels when editing, or tell when a draft was sent. Its Gmail permission would let it send or delete anything, so not sending is a rule we keep, not a boundary the mailbox enforces, which is why I send everything by hand.

sections.label: What the next debrief should say
sections.line: The next debrief: unchanged emails, waiting time, recurring decisions, and a narrow sending policy.
sections.para: These numbers are a baseline. Next: how many emails went out unchanged, how long drafts wait, which decisions recur and could become rules, and whether a narrow policy could let the agent send routine email, which depends on the tools more than on the agent.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: The numbers are the agent's; weekly figures a floor; replies generous; examples invented.
sections.para: The counts come from the agent's 18 October debrief, from Gmail and its logs. Weekly figures come from 169 of 178 emails. The reply rate includes colleagues and other agents. The screenshots are redrawn with invented names, and no recipient is named.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: The inbox agent's debrief, two redrawn screenshots, my voice note, and related inbox articles.
sections.para: The inbox agent's debrief Three weeks in the inbox, of 18 October 2026; the drafts folder and a decision draft, redrawn with invented examples; my voice note of that day; and related articles on the agentic inbox, the man behind the curtain, the jobs that never scaled, and hope or enforcement.
